title: The Lymphatic and Immune Systems
description: Week 12, matched to the instructor's Exam 4 study guide: the lymph nodes and vessels, the bone marrow, thymus, tonsils, and spleen, the white blood cells and what each does, antibodies, memory cells, and vaccines, inflammation and its markers, and supporting immune health, with a case study.

wound.intro: A nurse in an urgent care clinic is caring for a 68-year-old client with a painful, swollen lower leg.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
Nurses' Notes

Day 1, 0900: Client scraped the left shin on a garden fence 4 days ago. The area is now red, warm, swollen, and painful, about 10 cm across, with yellow drainage. Reports chills last night. Takes an herbal supplement “for immunity” and drinks two energy drinks a day. Has never had a pneumococcal vaccine. Walks the dog every day. Strong pulses in both ankles.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching how the body handles the small amount of fluid that leaks out of the blood capillaries into the tissues each day. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: Arterioles pull it back in at the start of the next heartbeat
The kidneys draw it out of the tissues and excrete it
Sweat glands carry it to the skin, where it evaporates
Lymphatic vessels collect it and return it to the veins
questions.rationale:
Fluid that leaks into the tissues is picked up by lymphatic capillaries, which begin as dead-end tubes in the tissues. As lymph, it's filtered through nodes and returned to the veins, keeping fluid in balance.

The kidneys aren't the right answer: they control the body's fluid, but they work on the blood, not directly on the fluid in the tissues.

Takeaway: The lymphatic system returns leaked tissue fluid to the blood; when it can't, the tissue swells.

questions.stem: After a client eats a meal high in fat, the lymph coming from the small intestine looks milky. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: White blood cells gather in the intestinal lining to digest the extra fat
Lacteals in the intestinal lining absorb dietary fats into the lymph
The liver sends bile into the lymph to break the fat down
The spleen releases stored fat into the lymph after a meal
questions.rationale:
Lacteals are lymphatic capillaries in the lining of the small intestine. They absorb dietary fats, which make the lymph there milky (chyle), and carry them toward the bloodstream.

Bile isn't the right answer: bile helps digest fat, but it's released into the intestine, not into the lymph.

Takeaway: Fat absorption is one of the lymphatic system's three jobs, through the lacteals.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how lymph moves. For each description, click to specify the structure it describes.
rows: Carries filtered lymph away from a lymph node
Drains lymph from the right arm and the right side of the head
Carries unfiltered lymph toward a lymph node
Drains lymph from both legs, the abdomen, and the left arm
questions.rationale:
Afferent vessels carry unfiltered lymph toward a node, and efferent vessels carry filtered lymph away. The right lymphatic duct drains the right upper body: the right arm, right upper trunk, and right side of the head and neck. The thoracic duct drains everything else.

Swapping afferent and efferent is a mistake. Think of afferent as arriving at the node and efferent as exiting it.

Takeaway: Afferent arrives, efferent exits. The right duct drains the right upper body; the thoracic duct drains the rest.

questions.stem: Place the path of fluid that leaves a capillary in the foot and returns to the blood in order.
items: Interstitial fluid around the cells of the foot
A vein at the base of the neck
questions.rationale:
Tissue fluid enters a lymphatic capillary, travels in an afferent vessel to a lymph node for filtering, leaves in an efferent vessel, and joins the thoracic duct, which empties into a vein at the base of the neck.

Placing the duct before the node is a mistake; the lymph is filtered in nodes along the way before it reaches the large ducts.

Takeaway: Tissue fluid, lymphatic capillary, afferent vessel, node, efferent vessel, duct, vein.

questions.stem: A tumor is blocking a client's thoracic duct. Which area should the nurse expect to still drain normally?
options: The left arm and the left side of the head, neck, and chest
Both legs and the lower abdomen
The right arm and the right side of the head and neck
The small intestine, including the lacteals
questions.rationale:
The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm, the right upper trunk, and the right side of the head and neck, so lymph from there doesn't pass through the thoracic duct and still drains.

The left arm and left side of the head aren't the right answer: they're also the upper body, but they drain through the thoracic duct, as do the legs, abdomen, and intestines.

Takeaway: Only the right upper body bypasses the thoracic duct, through the right lymphatic duct.

questions.stem: After a car crash, a client has fractures of the left 9th to 11th ribs, pain in the left upper abdomen, a heart rate of 124/min, and a blood pressure of 88/52 mm Hg. Which organ should the nurse suspect is bleeding?
options: The liver
The appendix
The gallbladder
The spleen
questions.rationale:
The spleen sits in the left upper abdomen, behind the left 9th to 11th ribs. It's spongy and full of blood, so an injury can bleed heavily, causing a fast heart rate and a falling blood pressure.

The liver isn't the right answer: it also bleeds heavily when injured, but it sits on the right side, under the right ribs.

Takeaway: Left lower rib fractures with signs of bleeding: think of the spleen.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the spleen. For each function, click to specify the part of the spleen that carries it out.
rows: Filters old and damaged red blood cells out of the blood
Produces and matures lymphocytes
Stores platelets and white blood cells for release when needed
Processes antigens to start an immune response
questions.rationale:
White pulp is the spleen's immune tissue: it produces and matures lymphocytes and processes antigens. Red pulp filters the blood, removing old red cells, and holds a reserve of white cells and platelets.

Linking stored white blood cells with the white pulp is a mistake: the names match, but the reserve is held in the red pulp.

Takeaway: White pulp: immune work. Red pulp: filtering and storage.

questions.stem: In the thymus, developing T cells that react strongly against the body's own tissues are destroyed. What does this process protect against?
options: Autoimmune disease
Allergic reactions to pollen
Viral infections
Lymphedema
questions.rationale:
This is negative selection: the thymus screens out T cells that would attack the body's own tissues, protecting against autoimmune disease.

Allergic reactions aren't the right answer: they're also unwanted immune responses, but they're overreactions to outside substances, like pollen, not attacks on the body's own cells.

Takeaway: The thymus removes self-attacking T cells, guarding against autoimmunity.

questions.stem: A child has frequent sore throats, and the provider mentions the tonsils. Which explanation of the tonsils' role should the nurse give?
options: They make the saliva that begins digesting food
They close the airway when the child swallows
They're lymphoid tissue that traps germs from the mouth and nose
They warm and moisten the air before it moves down into the lungs
questions.rationale:
The tonsils are lymphoid tissue at the back of the throat. They trap pathogens entering through the mouth and nose and start immune responses.

Closing the airway isn't the right answer: the tonsils sit near the throat, but that's the epiglottis's job.

Takeaway: Tonsils guard the entrance of the throat as lymphoid tissue.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how T cells mature in the thymus. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: In the thymus, {{0}} keeps the T cells that can recognize the body's own markers, and {{1}} destroys the T cells that would attack the body's own tissues.

options: clonal expansion
positive selection
phagocytosis
negative selection
opsonization
antigen presentation

questions.rationale:
Positive selection keeps T cells that can recognize the body's own markers, and negative selection removes those that react against the body's own tissues. Most developing T cells don't pass, and only those that pass both leave the thymus.

Clonal expansion isn't the right answer for the first blank: it also increases useful T cells, but it happens later, when mature T cells meet a pathogen.

Takeaway: Positive selection keeps useful T cells; negative selection removes self-attacking ones.

questions.stem: A client asks why an inflamed ankle is swollen. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “The injured muscle swells up as it gets stronger during healing.”
“Blood vessels in the ankle tighten up, which traps extra blood and fluid in the area.”
“The ankle's lymph nodes fill with fluid to fight the injury.”
“Chemicals like histamine make the small vessels leaky, so fluid moves into the tissue.”
questions.rationale:
Inflammatory mediators, like histamine and kinins, increase the permeability of the small vessels, so fluid and proteins leak into the tissue, causing swelling. Widened vessels also bring redness and warmth.

Vessels tightening isn't the right answer: it sounds like a way to trap fluid, but inflammation widens the vessels; that's what makes the area red and warm.

Takeaway: Inflammation: wider vessels bring redness and heat; leaky vessels bring swelling.

questions.stem: Place the steps by which white blood cells leave the blood to reach an infection in order.
items: Chemical signals attract white blood cells to the area
The cells roll along the inner wall of the vessel
The cells stick tightly to the vessel wall
The cells squeeze through the vessel wall into the tissue
questions.rationale:
Leukocyte extravasation goes: chemoattraction, rolling adhesion, tight adhesion, and transmigration through the vessel wall into the tissue.

Putting the tight adhesion first is a mistake; cells have to slow down by rolling before they can stick firmly.

Takeaway: Attract, roll, stick, squeeze through.

questions.stem: A client develops itchy, raised welts (hives) after eating shellfish. Which cells should the nurse recognize as the source of the histamine causing the itching and swelling?
options: Red blood cells in the circulation
Mast cells in the skin and tissues
Platelets at the site of the welts
Neutrophils arriving from the blood
questions.rationale:
Mast cells are resident cells in the tissues that act as sentinels. When triggered, they release histamine, which makes vessels leaky and causes itching and swelling, as in hives.

Neutrophils aren't the right answer: they're the most common white cells, but they fight acute bacterial infection by phagocytosis; histamine comes from mast cells and basophils.

Takeaway: Histamine comes from mast cells and basophils: itching, leaky vessels, and swelling.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client's wound for signs of acute inflammation. Which findings should the nurse expect?
options: Redness
Coolness of the skin
Swelling
Numbness
Pain
Warmth
questions.rationale:
The signs of acute inflammation are redness and warmth (from widened vessels), swelling (from leaky vessels), pain (from mediators like kinins), and loss of function.

Numbness isn't the right answer: swelling can press on nerves, but inflammation typically causes pain, not numbness. Coolness is the opposite of what widened vessels bring.

Takeaway: Inflammation: redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the lymphocytes. For each function, click to specify the lymphocyte that carries it out.
rows: Makes antibodies after it becomes a plasma cell
Directly kills virus-infected and cancer cells
Keeps immune cells from attacking the body's own cells
Activates B cells and killer T cells
questions.rationale:
B cells become plasma cells that make antibodies (humoral immunity). Killer (CD8+) T cells directly kill infected and cancer cells. Helper (CD4+) T cells activate B cells and killer T cells. Regulatory T cells keep the immune system from attacking the body.

Giving antibody production to the helper T cells is a mistake: they're needed for it, but they activate the B cells, which make the antibodies.

Takeaway: B cells make antibodies; CD8+ T cells kill; CD4+ T cells help; regulatory T cells restrain.

questions.stem: Which cells in the lungs engulf inhaled dust and microbes?
options: Alveolar macrophages
Kupffer cells
Microglia
Plasma cells
questions.rationale:
Macrophages, which develop from monocytes, have different names in different tissues: alveolar macrophages in the lungs, Kupffer cells in the liver, and microglia in the nervous system.

Kupffer cells aren't the right answer: they're also macrophages, but they live in the liver.

Takeaway: Macrophages by location: alveolar (lungs), Kupffer (liver), microglia (nervous system).

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing dendritic cells. Which description of their role should the nurse give?
options: They make antibodies that circulate in the blood and lymph
They release heparin to keep the blood from clotting at an infection site
They form scar tissue after an infection heals
They capture antigens in the tissues and carry them to the lymph nodes
questions.rationale:
Dendritic cells live in tissues that meet the outside world, like the skin, nose, lungs, and intestines. They capture antigens, migrate to the lymph nodes, and present them to T cells, linking innate and adaptive immunity.

Making antibodies isn't the right answer: dendritic cells start the specific response, but antibodies come from B cells (plasma cells).

Takeaway: Dendritic cells are messengers: they carry antigens from the tissues to T cells in the nodes.

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has a very low neutrophil count. Which risk should the nurse focus on?
options: Bleeding, since neutrophils help blood clot
Allergic reactions, since neutrophils control the release of histamine
Anemia, since neutrophils carry oxygen
Infection, since neutrophils are the first defense against bacteria
questions.rationale:
Neutrophils, 50% to 70% of white cells, are the first to reach an infection and destroy bacteria by phagocytosis. Too few means a high risk of infection.

Bleeding isn't the right answer: chemotherapy can lower platelets too, but platelets, not neutrophils, help blood clot.

Takeaway: Low neutrophils mean high infection risk; low platelets mean bleeding risk.

questions.stem: A client vaccinated against measles is exposed to the virus but doesn't get sick. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: The vaccine's antibodies stay in the blood for life
The vaccine made the client's innate defenses stronger and faster
Memory cells from the vaccine respond quickly to the virus
The virus can't enter the cells of a vaccinated person
questions.rationale:
A vaccine trains the adaptive immune system, which keeps memory B and T cells. On exposure, they recognize the virus and respond quickly and strongly, before it can cause illness.

Antibodies staying for life isn't the right answer: antibodies fade over time; protection lasts because memory cells can quickly make more.

Takeaway: Vaccines work through memory: a faster, stronger response the next time.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the classes of antibodies (immunoglobulins). For each description, click to specify the antibody.
rows: Found in tears, saliva, and breast milk
The first antibody made after a new exposure
The most common antibody in the blood
Defends against parasites and triggers allergic reactions
questions.rationale:
IgA protects body secretions, like tears, saliva, and colostrum. IgM is the first antibody made in a new response. IgG is the most common antibody in the blood, about 75%. IgE defends against parasites and drives allergic reactions.

Calling IgG the first antibody is a mistake: it's the most common, but IgM comes first and IgG follows.

Takeaway: IgA in secretions, IgM first, IgG most common, IgE for parasites and allergy.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks the difference between an antigen and an antibody. Which response is accurate?
options: “An antigen is a protein made by B cells, and an antibody is a marker found on a germ.”
“An antigen is a marker on a germ or cell; an antibody is a protein that binds it.”
“Antigens and antibodies are two names for the same protective protein.”
“An antigen is a type of white blood cell; an antibody is what it releases.”
questions.rationale:
An antigen is a marker, found on viruses, bacteria, tumors, and the body's own cells, that the immune system recognizes. An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a protective protein that binds to a specific antigen.

Reversing the two isn't the right answer, even though the words sound alike; remember that the antibody acts against the antigen.

Takeaway: Antigen: the marker. Antibody: the protein that binds it.

questions.stem: A client asks, “Why did I get so sick from a new virus before my body fought it off?” Which response should the nurse give?
options: “Your body had no defenses against it until you took a medicine for it.”
“The virus shut down your immune system for the whole first week of the illness.”
“Your body's specific defenses take 4 to 7 days to build up against a new germ.”
“Your body starts fighting a virus after you've had a fever for several days.”
questions.rationale:
The innate immune system responds right away, but the adaptive system, which targets a specific germ, takes about 4 to 7 days to mount a strong response the first time. After that, memory cells make later responses faster.

No defenses until the medicine isn't the right answer: the client felt so sick, but innate defenses were working from the start; the specific response just takes days.

Takeaway: First exposure: innate right away, adaptive in about 4 to 7 days. Later exposures: memory makes it fast.

questions.stem: A client with severe influenza develops a high fever, widespread inflammation, and failing organs. The provider describes a cytokine storm. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: The immune system releases cytokines out of control, harming its own tissues
The virus releases toxins that keep the client's cytokines from working normally
The client's immune system has stopped producing cytokines
The client's antibodies are attacking the influenza vaccine
questions.rationale:
A cytokine storm (hypercytokinemia) is an uncontrolled release of cytokines by the immune system. The inflammation it causes can damage organs; it has been seen in severe influenza, COVID-19, and acute pancreatitis.

Stopped producing cytokines isn't the right answer: the client is so sick, but the problem is too much of the immune response, not too little.

Takeaway: A cytokine storm is the immune system overreacting, harming the body it's protecting.

questions.stem: A client with HIV asks why the infection makes it hard to fight off other germs. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “HIV infects and destroys helper T cells, which direct the rest of the immune system.”
“HIV destroys your red blood cells, so less oxygen reaches the immune cells.”
“HIV blocks your skin from acting as a barrier against germs.”
“HIV makes your body produce too many antibodies, which slowly wear out the immune system.”
questions.rationale:
HIV invades helper (CD4+) T cells. As their number falls, B cells and killer T cells aren't activated well, and cell-mediated immunity weakens, so other infections take hold.

Too many antibodies isn't the right answer: the immune system is clearly involved, but the problem is the loss of helper T cells that coordinate the response.

Takeaway: HIV destroys CD4+ helper T cells, which weakens the whole adaptive response.

questions.stem: Leukemia cells have filled a client's bone marrow, crowding out the normal cells. Which findings should the nurse expect?
options: Fatigue from fewer red cells, with normal white cells
Clots in the legs from too many platelets
Frequent infections, easy bruising, and fatigue
Swollen neck nodes, with normal blood counts
questions.rationale:
The bone marrow makes all the blood cells: red cells, white cells, and platelets. When it's crowded out, all three fall: fewer white cells (infections), fewer platelets (bruising and bleeding), and fewer red cells (fatigue).

Fatigue with normal white cells isn't the right answer: anemia is the best-known effect, but the marrow makes every blood cell line, so all of them drop.

Takeaway: Bone marrow failure lowers red cells, white cells, and platelets together.

questions.stem: A client scheduled for a bone marrow biopsy asks what the marrow does. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “It makes all your blood cells, and it's where B cells mature.”
“It filters your blood and removes your old red cells.”
“It's where your T cells mature and learn to spare your body.”
“It filters lymph and traps germs before they reach the blood.”
questions.rationale:
All blood cells form from stem cells in the bone marrow, and B cells also mature there.

Where T cells mature isn't the right answer: T cells do form in the marrow, but they mature in the thymus. Filtering the blood is the spleen's job, and filtering lymph is the lymph nodes'.

Takeaway: Bone marrow: all blood cells form there; B cells mature there; T cells mature in the thymus.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing where white blood cells mature. For each cell, click to specify where it finishes maturing.
rows: Mast cell
Neutrophil
T cell
Macrophage (from a monocyte)
B cell
questions.rationale:
Every white cell starts in the bone marrow. Neutrophils and B cells finish maturing there; T cells finish in the thymus; mast cell precursors and monocytes leave the blood and mature in the tissues (monocytes become macrophages).

Putting T cells in the bone marrow is a mistake, even though that's where they're made. Their training happens in the thymus.

Takeaway: Marrow: neutrophils, B cells. Thymus: T cells. Tissues: mast cells, macrophages.

questions.stem: A client with allergic asthma has a high eosinophil count. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: Eosinophils join in allergy and asthma reactions, so they rise
Eosinophils fight bacteria, so the asthma must be from an infection
Eosinophils make antibodies, so the body is building immunity
Eosinophils carry oxygen, so they rise when breathing is hard
questions.rationale:
Eosinophils fight parasites and take part in allergic reactions and asthma, so a high count fits allergic asthma.

Fighting bacteria isn't the right answer: a high white count often means infection, but bacteria raise neutrophils.

Takeaway: Eosinophils: parasites, allergies, asthma.

questions.stem: A nurse is comparing basophils and mast cells, since both release histamine. Which statement about them is accurate?
options: Basophils stay in the tissues; mast cells circulate in the blood
Both are lymphocytes that make antibodies against allergens
Both mature in the thymus before they enter the bloodstream
Basophils circulate in the blood; mast cells stay in the tissues
questions.rationale:
Basophils travel in the blood; mast cells live in the tissues (skin, airways, gut) as sentinels. Both release histamine, which makes vessels leaky and causes itching and swelling.

The reversed pair isn't the right answer, even though the two cells are so alike. Remember that mast cells sit in place, guarding the tissues.

Takeaway: Basophils in the blood, mast cells in the tissues: both release histamine.

questions.stem: A client has had a long-lasting infection, and the monocyte count is high. Which role should the nurse expect these monocytes to play once they reach the infected tissue?
options: They become plasma cells that release antibodies
They become macrophages that engulf germs and dead cells
They release histamine that makes the nearby vessels leaky
They kill virus-infected cells without engulfing them
questions.rationale:
Monocytes leave the blood and become macrophages (or dendritic cells) in the tissues. Macrophages engulf germs, dead cells, and debris, and show antigens to T cells.

Plasma cells aren't the right answer: they also develop from cells in the blood, but plasma cells come from B cells.

Takeaway: Monocytes become macrophages: the big eaters of the tissues.

questions.stem: A client's infected wound is draining thick, yellow pus. Which explanation of what pus is made of should the nurse give?
options: Dead red blood cells mixed with plasma
Antibodies that have bound tightly to the bacteria
Extra lymph that leaked from nearby nodes
Dead neutrophils, bacteria, and damaged tissue
questions.rationale:
Neutrophils are the first white cells to arrive and engulf bacteria; they die quickly, and their remains, with the bacteria and damaged tissue, form pus.

Antibodies isn't the right answer: they bind bacteria too, but they're proteins dissolved in fluid, not the thick material of pus.

Takeaway: Pus is mostly dead neutrophils: a sign they've been fighting bacteria.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the stages of inflammation. For each description, click to specify the stage.
rows: Lasts about 2 to 6 weeks as healing continues
Is often quiet, but is linked to heart disease and diabetes
Starts within minutes of a cut, with redness, warmth, and swelling
Neutrophils are the first white cells to arrive
Goes on for months, with macrophages and lymphocytes causing slow damage
questions.rationale:
Acute inflammation starts within minutes to hours and lasts days: redness, warmth, swelling, and pain, with neutrophils arriving first, then macrophages. Subacute inflammation lasts about 2 to 6 weeks. Chronic inflammation lasts months or longer; macrophages and lymphocytes keep it going, and it's linked to heart disease, diabetes, and arthritis.

Calling chronic inflammation the red, swollen kind is a mistake. Chronic inflammation is usually low-grade and quiet.

Takeaway: Acute: fast and red, neutrophils. Subacute: 2 to 6 weeks. Chronic: quiet and long, macrophages and lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the cytokines of inflammation. For each action, click to specify the cytokine group that performs it.
rows: Released by virus-infected cells to warn the cells nearby
Form a trail that draws neutrophils to an infection
Made mostly by macrophages; very large amounts can cause shock
Carry messages between white cells; some cause fever
questions.rationale:
Interferons come from virus-infected cells and help nearby cells resist the virus. Chemokines call white cells to a site. Tumor necrosis factor, mostly from macrophages, drives inflammation and fever, and too much at once can cause shock. Interleukins pass messages between white cells; IL-1 and IL-6 cause fever.

Mixing up chemokines and interleukins is a mistake, even though both are messages. Chemokines specifically make cells move toward the site.

Takeaway: Chemokines call, interferons fight viruses, interleukins message, TNF inflames.

questions.stem: A client asks how the immune system can recognize a new virus it has never met before. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Your immune cells copy the virus's shape after it infects you, and then attack it.”
“Each of your B and T cells has its own receptor, so some match almost any germ.”
“The antibodies from your past infections attach to any new virus that enters.”
“Your body spots a new virus by its size, since viruses look alike.”
questions.rationale:
This is the result of heterogeneity: as lymphocytes develop, their receptor genes are shuffled and mutated, so each B and T cell carries a unique receptor. With so much variety, some cells match almost any germ, and those cells multiply when it appears.

Copying the virus's shape isn't the right answer: the response is so specific, but the matching receptors already exist before the virus arrives; the virus selects them.

Takeaway: Receptor variety (heterogeneity) lets the immune system recognize germs it has never seen.

questions.stem: Two coworkers get the same vaccine. One makes high antibody levels, and the other makes much lower levels. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: People's immune responses vary with their genes, age, and health
The coworker with low levels must have had the infection already
The coworker with low levels is likely allergic to the vaccine
Antibody levels depend on which arm the vaccine was given in
questions.rationale:
The immune response is heterogeneous: people differ in their receptor genes, age, and health (for example, older adults and people on immune-suppressing drugs often respond less strongly), so the same vaccine can give different antibody levels.

A past infection isn't the right answer: that would usually make the response stronger, since memory cells are already there.

Takeaway: People respond differently to the same germ or vaccine: one result of heterogeneity.

questions.stem: Two days after starting antibiotics for an infection, a client's C-reactive protein (CRP) has fallen by half, but the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is still high. How should the nurse interpret this?
options: The infection is getting worse, since the ESR is still high
The inflammation is easing; the ESR falls more slowly than CRP
The CRP result must be wrong, since both should fall together
A new infection has started, since the two results disagree
questions.rationale:
CRP rises within hours and falls quickly once inflammation settles. The ESR rises and falls more slowly, so it often lags behind. A falling CRP with a still-high ESR fits inflammation that's improving.

The infection is getting worse isn't the right answer: the ESR is still high, but the faster-moving CRP is the better sign of the current trend.

Takeaway: CRP changes fast; ESR changes slowly. Follow the trend.

questions.stem: A client has a fever and a cough, and the provider orders a procalcitonin level. Which explanation of the test should the nurse give?
options: “It measures how fast your red cells settle in a tube, which shows inflammation.”
“It's a stress hormone level that shows how your body is coping.”
“It rises mostly with bacterial infections, which helps guide antibiotics.”
“It shows whether your prostate is inflamed or enlarged.”
questions.rationale:
Procalcitonin stays very low in health and rises sharply in bacterial infections and sepsis, while staying low in most viral infections. It helps the provider decide whether antibiotics are likely to help.

How fast red cells settle isn't the right answer: it's another inflammation test, but that's the ESR, which doesn't tell bacteria from other causes.

Takeaway: Procalcitonin points toward bacterial infection; CRP and ESR show inflammation of any cause.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client with a fever, pain on urination, and a tender prostate has a high prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level. The client asks whether this means cancer. Which response should the nurse give?
options: “Yes; a high PSA level confirms that you have prostate cancer.”
“No; PSA rises with age and isn't linked to the prostate.”
“PSA rises with infections anywhere in the body, so it says little about the prostate.”
“An inflamed prostate can raise PSA too; the provider will follow up.”
questions.rationale:
PSA is made by normal and cancerous prostate cells. Cancer can raise it, but so can prostatitis (inflammation) and an enlarged prostate (BPH). With signs of prostatitis, the high PSA needs follow-up, not a conclusion.

“A high PSA confirms cancer” isn't the right answer: PSA is used to screen for prostate cancer, but it isn't specific to cancer.

Takeaway: PSA rises with prostate cancer, BPH, and prostatitis.

questions.stem: A healthy 68-year-old client had all childhood vaccines. Which vaccines should the nurse recommend now?
options: No more vaccines, since childhood vaccines protect for a lifetime
Pneumococcal, shingles, and yearly flu and COVID-19 vaccines
A shingles vaccine alone, since it also protects against pneumonia
A tetanus booster alone, since the others are for children
questions.rationale:
The instructor's list: keep up with vaccines and a record of them: childhood vaccines, yearly flu and COVID-19 vaccines, and pneumococcal and shingles vaccines for older adults.

No more vaccines isn't the right answer: the client is healthy, but protection from some childhood vaccines fades, and older adults face new risks like shingles and pneumonia.

Takeaway: Older adults: pneumococcal and shingles, plus yearly flu and COVID-19.

questions.stem: A college student drinks three energy drinks a day to stay awake for studying. Which explanation of how this affects health should the nurse give?
options: “Their caffeine strengthens your white cells against infection.”
“They supply the vitamins your immune cells need, so diet matters less.”
“Their sugar and artificial ingredients can promote inflammation.”
“They affect your sleep, but they have no effect on inflammation.”
questions.rationale:
The instructor's guide names energy drinks as a lifestyle choice that harms health: they're high in sugar and artificial ingredients, which can lead to inflammation.

Supplying vitamins isn't the right answer: some drinks add vitamins, but they don't replace whole foods, and the sugar works against the immune system.

Takeaway: Energy drinks: sugar and additives that promote inflammation.

questions.stem: A client says, “I take an herbal supplement for my immune system, so I don't need a flu shot.” Which response should the nurse give?
options: “Use supplements only with your provider's guidance, and keep getting vaccines.”
“That's fine; herbal supplements protect you just as well as the flu shot does.”
“Herbal supplements are natural, so you can take as much as you like.”
“Stop the supplement, since herbs weaken the immune system.”
questions.rationale:
The instructor's guide: herbal supplements can support immune health with the provider's guidance, as part of other healthy choices (exercise, a healthy diet, and vaccinations), never in place of them. Some interact with medications.

“Stop the supplement” isn't the right answer: it sounds cautious, but the nurse's role is to involve the provider, not to forbid it; the key teaching is that it doesn't replace the vaccine.

Takeaway: Supplements: with the provider's guidance, alongside vaccines, diet, and exercise.

questions.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' notes that need follow-up.
questions.passage: Client [[scraped the left shin on a garden fence 4 days ago]]. The area is now [[red, warm, swollen, and painful]], [[about 10 cm across]], with [[yellow drainage]]. [[Reports chills last night]]. [[Takes an herbal supplement “for immunity”]] and [[drinks two energy drinks a day]]. [[Has never had a pneumococcal vaccine]]. [[Walks the dog every day]]. [[Strong pulses in both ankles]].
questions.rationale:
The red, warm, swollen, painful area with drainage and chills shows acute inflammation from an infection that's spreading into the body; its size is a baseline to track. The supplement needs the provider's review, the energy drinks feed inflammation, and the missing pneumococcal vaccine is a prevention gap.

The scrape on the fence doesn't need follow-up: it started everything, but it's the history, not something to act on now. Daily walks and strong pulses are reassuring.

Takeaway: Act on the signs of inflammation and infection, then the gaps in immune health.

questions.stem: For each laboratory result, click to specify what it most likely shows.
rows: White blood cells 15,800/mm³, with 82% neutrophils
C-reactive protein 9.6 mg/dL
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 48 mm/hr
Procalcitonin 1.8 ng/mL
Hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL
questions.rationale:
A high white count driven by neutrophils, and a high procalcitonin, point to a bacterial infection. CRP and ESR show that inflammation is present but not its cause. The hemoglobin is normal.

Reading a high CRP as proof of bacteria is a mistake. CRP rises with any inflammation; procalcitonin is the more specific clue.

Takeaway: Neutrophils and procalcitonin: bacteria. CRP and ESR: inflammation of any cause.

questions.stem: Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: The red, warm, swollen leg shows {{0}} inflammation. The white cells that arrive first are {{1}}, drawn to the site by {{2}}.

options: chronic
acute
subacute
macrophages
lymphocytes
neutrophils
chemokines
interferons
antibodies

questions.rationale:
Redness, warmth, swelling, and pain within days of an injury are acute inflammation. Neutrophils arrive first, followed by macrophages, following the trail of chemokines to the site.

Macrophages isn't the right answer: they're key to inflammation, but they arrive after the neutrophils and clean up.

Takeaway: Acute inflammation: neutrophils first, called in by chemokines.

questions.stem: Before the client leaves, which teaching about immune health should the nurse include?
options: Ask the provider before continuing the herbal supplement
Replace the energy drinks with water
Ask about getting the pneumococcal vaccine
Eat mostly whole foods, like vegetables, fruits, and whole grains
Stop walking the dog for the next month
Double the herbal supplement while the infection lasts
questions.rationale:
The instructor's interventions: supplements with the provider's guidance, vaccinations (pneumococcal for older adults), a whole-food diet, and regular exercise; energy drinks promote inflammation.

Stopping the walks isn't the right answer: the leg is sore, but regular exercise supports immune health; the client can rest the leg as the provider directs without giving up activity for a month.

Takeaway: Teach vaccines, whole foods, exercise, and supplements only with the provider's guidance.

questions.stem: Three days after starting antibiotics, the client returns. For each finding, click to specify whether it has improved, not changed, or gotten worse.
rows: Temperature: 38.6 °C then, 37.0 °C now
C-reactive protein: 9.6 mg/dL then, 3.1 mg/dL now
Procalcitonin: 1.8 ng/mL then, 0.4 ng/mL now
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 48 mm/hr then, 47 mm/hr now
Red area: 10 cm across then, 14 cm across now
questions.rationale:
The fever, CRP, and procalcitonin are all falling, which fits an infection responding to treatment. The ESR hasn't changed, which is expected, since it falls slowly. But the red area has grown, so the infection may be spreading at the edges: report it.

Calling everything improved because the labs are better is a mistake. A spreading area of redness needs follow-up even when the numbers improve.

Takeaway: Read every finding: improving markers don't cancel a spreading infection.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing where lymph drains. For each infection, click to specify the lymph node group most likely to swell.
rows: Strep throat
An infected cut on the hand
An infected ingrown toenail
An abscessed tooth
A skin infection on the lower leg
questions.rationale:
Nodes swell near the area they drain: the throat, mouth, and teeth drain to the cervical nodes in the neck; the hand and arm to the axillary nodes in the armpit; and the foot and leg to the inguinal nodes in the groin.

Putting the toenail with the axillary nodes is a mistake: the axillary group is large, but the foot drains to the inguinal nodes.

Takeaway: Throat and teeth → cervical, arm → axillary, leg → inguinal.

questions.stem: A client has an infected cut on the left foot, with red streaks running up the leg. Which finding should the nurse expect when palpating the lymph nodes?
options: Tender, enlarged nodes in the right groin
Tender, enlarged nodes in the left armpit
Tender, enlarged nodes in the left groin
Tender, enlarged nodes on the left side of the neck
questions.rationale:
Lymph from the foot and leg drains to the inguinal nodes in the groin on the same side, so a left-foot infection enlarges the left groin nodes, which become tender as their lymphocytes respond. The red streaks are lymphangitis, inflammation of the lymph vessels carrying the infection toward those nodes.

The right groin isn't the right answer: lymph drains to the nodes on the same side. The armpit and neck nodes drain the arm and the head.

Takeaway: Foot and leg infections: inguinal nodes, on the same side.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how lymph returns to the blood. Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: Lymph from the legs, the abdomen, the left arm, and the left side of the head and chest returns to the blood through the {{0}}, which empties into a vein at the base of the neck on the {{1}} side. The {{2}} drains the right upper part of the body.

options: thoracic duct
right lymphatic duct
cisterna chyli
right
left
cisterna chyli
right lymphatic duct
thoracic duct

questions.rationale:
The thoracic duct rises from the cisterna chyli in the abdomen and carries lymph from the legs, abdomen, left arm, and left side of the head and chest, emptying into a vein at the base of the neck on the left. The short right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and the right side of the head and chest.

The cisterna chyli isn't the right answer for the first blank: it collects lymph from the intestines and lower body, but it's where the thoracic duct begins, not where lymph returns to the blood.

Takeaway: Thoracic duct: most of the body, into the left side of the neck. Right lymphatic duct: the right upper part.

questions.stem: After a blow to the left side of the abdomen, a client has tenderness in the left upper quadrant, under the ribs. Which lymphatic organ lies in this area?
options: The thymus
The spleen
The liver
The appendix
questions.rationale:
The spleen, the largest lymphatic organ, lies in the left upper quadrant, under the lower left ribs and the diaphragm. It filters the blood, holds lymphocytes and macrophages, and stores red cells and platelets, and a blow there can injure it and cause bleeding.

The liver isn't the right answer: it lies mostly on the right side, and it isn't a lymphatic organ. The thymus is in the upper chest, and the appendix, which has lymphoid tissue, is in the right lower quadrant.

Takeaway: The spleen: the largest lymphatic organ, in the left upper quadrant under the ribs.

questions.stem: A client asks how lymph moves through the body without a pump like the heart. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “The heart pumps it through a separate chamber of its own.”
“Gravity carries it upward from the legs to the neck.”
“Muscles squeeze the vessels, and valves keep it moving one way.”
“The lymph nodes contract in a steady rhythm to push it forward.”
questions.rationale:
Lymph vessels have valves, and the squeeze of skeletal muscles (and the pressure changes of breathing) push lymph along, one way, toward the neck.

The heart doesn't pump lymph, gravity works against flow from the legs, and the nodes filter lymph rather than pump it.

Takeaway: Lymph moves by muscle squeezes, breathing, and one-way valves; movement helps it flow.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks what lymph is. Which answer should the nurse give?
options: “Tissue fluid that enters lymph vessels and returns to the blood.”
“Blood plasma that still carries its red blood cells with it.”
“Fluid that flows away from the heart through the arteries.”
“A fluid the spleen makes for the lymph nodes to fight infection.”
questions.rationale:
Lymph is the fluid that leaks from the capillaries into the tissues, enters the lymph vessels, and is returned to the blood near the heart.

Lymph has no red cells, it flows in lymph vessels rather than arteries, and the spleen filters blood instead of making lymph.

Takeaway: Lymph: tissue fluid on its way back to the blood.

questions.stem: A client asks why the lymph nodes near an infection swell. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: When germs carried in the lymph reach a node, the {{0}} inside it multiply to fight them, and the node {{1}}.

options: red blood cells
lymphocytes
platelets
shrinks and hardens
empties into the thoracic duct
swells and becomes tender

questions.rationale:
Lymph nodes filter the lymph. When they catch germs, their lymphocytes multiply, and the node swells and becomes tender.

Choosing red blood cells is a mistake: nodes hold lymphocytes and macrophages, not red cells.

Takeaway: Swollen, tender node near an infection: lymphocytes at work.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing lymph drainage. For each body area, click to specify the duct its lymph drains into.
rows: The right arm
The left arm
Both legs
The right side of the head
The abdomen
questions.rationale:
The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and the right side of the head and chest. The thoracic duct drains everything else: the left arm, both legs, and the abdomen.

Sending the right leg's lymph to the right lymphatic duct is a mistake: both legs drain into the thoracic duct.

Takeaway: Right upper quarter: right lymphatic duct. The rest: thoracic duct.

questions.stem: A client with breast cancer asks why the surgeon will check the lymph nodes in the armpit. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “The lymph nodes make the cancer cells, so they need to be removed.”
“Cancer cells can travel in the lymph and lodge in nearby nodes.”
“The nodes supply blood to the breast tissue around the tumor.”
“Checking the nodes shows how well your heart is pumping.”
questions.rationale:
Lymph from the breast drains to the armpit (axillary) nodes, so cancer cells that spread through the lymph often reach those nodes first.

The nodes don't make cancer cells or supply blood to the breast, and they don't reflect how the heart pumps.

Takeaway: Nodes filter lymph, so they can catch spreading cancer cells.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the lymphatic system. Which of the following are its functions?
options: Carrying oxygen out to the body's tissues
Filtering germs in the lymph nodes
Pumping blood through the lungs and body
Absorbing fats from the small intestine
Returning tissue fluid to the blood
questions.rationale:
The lymphatic system returns tissue fluid to the blood, absorbs fats through the lacteals of the small intestine, and filters germs in the lymph nodes.

Pumping blood is the heart's job, and carrying oxygen is the red cells' job.

Takeaway: Lymphatic jobs: fluid return, fat absorption, defense.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing lymph nodes. Which cells inside a node attack the germs filtered from the lymph?
options: Red blood cells and platelets
Mast cells and basophils
Lymphocytes and macrophages
Type 2 alveolar cells
questions.rationale:
Lymph nodes are packed with lymphocytes (T and B cells) and macrophages, which recognize and destroy the germs the node filters.

Red cells and platelets aren't defense cells. Mast cells and basophils release histamine in tissues and blood, and type 2 cells are in the alveoli.

Takeaway: Lymph nodes: lymphocytes and macrophages.

questions.stem: A client had the spleen removed after an injury. Which risk should the nurse teach the client about?
options: A higher risk of serious infections, from certain bacteria
A higher risk of bleeding from a lack of platelets
A lower red blood cell count for the rest of the client's life
A lower ability to absorb fats from food
questions.rationale:
The spleen filters germs from the blood, so without it the risk of serious infections rises, especially from certain bacteria (like pneumococcus); vaccines matter more.

Platelets often rise after the spleen is removed, red cells are still made in the bone marrow, and fat absorption happens in the gut's lacteals.

Takeaway: No spleen: watch for infection, keep vaccines current.

questions.stem: A client with mononucleosis has an enlarged spleen and asks about playing football. Which response should the nurse give?
options: “Play, but wear a brace around your knees and ankles for protection.”
“Contact sports are fine as soon as your sore throat is gone.”
“Football is fine, since your ribs protect the enlarged spleen from blows.”
“Avoid contact sports until cleared, since a swollen spleen can rupture.”
questions.rationale:
An enlarged spleen pushes below the ribs and is fragile; a blow can rupture it and cause serious bleeding, so contact sports wait until the provider clears the client.

An enlarged spleen extends past the ribs' protection. A knee brace doesn't protect it, and the spleen can stay enlarged after the sore throat is gone.

Takeaway: Big spleen: no contact sports until cleared.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the lymphoid organs. Which one filters the blood, rather than the lymph?
options: The tonsils
The thymus
The lymph nodes
The spleen
questions.rationale:
The spleen filters the blood: it removes old red cells and germs and holds immune cells.

The lymph nodes filter lymph, the tonsils trap germs entering the mouth and nose, and the thymus is where T cells mature.

Takeaway: Spleen: blood. Nodes: lymph.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the lymphoid organs. For each organ, click to specify its main role.
columns: Filters the blood and removes old red cells
Traps germs entering the mouth and nose
Makes blood cells; B cells mature here
rows: The spleen
The bone marrow
The thymus
The tonsils
The lymph nodes
questions.rationale:
The thymus matures T cells, the spleen filters the blood, the lymph nodes filter lymph, the tonsils guard the mouth and nose, and the bone marrow makes blood cells and matures B cells.

Giving the thymus the job of making all blood cells is a mistake: that's the bone marrow.

Takeaway: Marrow makes, thymus trains T cells, nodes and spleen filter, tonsils guard.

questions.stem: An adult's thymus is removed with a tumor. Which statement about the effect on the immune system is accurate?
options: The client can no longer make any antibodies
The client will need lifelong red blood cell transfusions
The client already has mature T cells, so the change is small
The client's lymph nodes will stop filtering lymph
questions.rationale:
The thymus does most of its work early in life, training T cells that then live in the nodes and spleen. An adult already has mature T cells, so losing the thymus has a small effect.

Antibodies come from B cells, red cells from the marrow, and the nodes keep filtering without the thymus.

Takeaway: Thymus: most active in childhood; it shrinks after puberty.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing where lymphocytes mature. Which organs should the nurse identify?
options: The spleen and the lymph nodes
The tonsils and the appendix
The liver and the kidneys
The bone marrow and the thymus
questions.rationale:
Lymphocytes mature in the bone marrow (B cells) and the thymus (T cells), the primary lymphoid organs.

The spleen, nodes, and tonsils are where mature lymphocytes meet germs. The liver and kidneys aren't lymphoid organs.

Takeaway: Mature in the marrow and thymus; work in the nodes, spleen, and tonsils.

questions.stem: A client's enlarged spleen is removing too many blood cells. Which findings should the nurse expect?
options: Low red cell and platelet counts
High red cell and platelet counts
A high white cell count with a fever
High levels of antibodies in the blood
questions.rationale:
An overactive spleen removes too many cells from the blood, so the red cell and platelet counts (and sometimes the white cells) are low.

Removing more cells lowers the counts, not raises them. A high white count with fever suggests infection, and the spleen's filtering doesn't raise antibodies.

Takeaway: Overactive spleen: low counts.

questions.stem: A client asks what inflammation is. Which statement should the nurse include?
options: “It's how the body protects an injured area and starts repair.”
“It's an infection that has spread to the bloodstream.”
“It's the immune system attacking healthy tissue for no reason.”
“It's the body's way of shutting down blood flow to an injury.”
questions.rationale:
Inflammation is the body's protective response to injury or infection: blood flow increases and white cells and fluid reach the site to contain the damage and start repair.

It isn't an infection in the blood, it usually isn't an attack on healthy tissue, and blood flow to the area increases.

Takeaway: Inflammation: protect, clean up, repair.

questions.stem: A client with an infection asks why they have a fever. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Your white cells release heat as they engulf the germs.”
“Interleukins raise your brain's set point for body temperature.”
“Your muscles stop working, so your body traps heat.”
“The germs give off heat as they multiply in your blood and tissues.”
questions.rationale:
Interleukins and other cytokines reset the hypothalamus's set point, so the body holds in heat; the higher temperature slows some germs and speeds up immune cells.

Engulfing germs doesn't make the fever, the muscles keep working (shivering even makes heat), and the germs don't heat the blood.

Takeaway: Fever: cytokines reset the thermostat.

questions.stem: A client asks why an inflamed wound hurts. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Swelling presses on nerves, and injury chemicals irritate them.”
“The white cells bite into the nerve endings as they fight the germs.”
“The extra blood flow overheats the nerves in the wound.”
“The fever makes the nerves across your body more sensitive.”
questions.rationale:
Swelling presses on nerves, and chemicals released by the injured tissue (like prostaglandins and bradykinin) irritate the nerve endings.

White cells don't attack nerves, the extra blood doesn't overheat them, and a local wound can hurt without any fever.

Takeaway: Inflammatory pain: pressure plus chemical irritation.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's joint inflammation. Which findings suggest it has become chronic?
options: Lymphocytes and macrophages fill the area
Scar tissue is forming in the joint
It has lasted for several months
The symptoms began 2 hours ago
Neutrophils fill the joint fluid
questions.rationale:
Chronic inflammation lasts months, with lymphocytes and macrophages in the tissue and ongoing damage and repair that leave scar tissue.

Neutrophils and a start hours ago are features of acute inflammation.

Takeaway: Acute: hours to days, neutrophils. Chronic: months, lymphocytes and macrophages, scarring.

questions.stem: A client's inflamed knee can't bend fully. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “The inflammation has fused the bones of the knee together.”
“Swelling and pain limit the movement, a sign of inflammation.”
“The cartilage has dissolved, so the joint is locked in place.”
“The knee is protecting itself by tightening the muscles around it.”
questions.rationale:
Loss of function is a sign of inflammation: swelling and pain limit how far the joint can move.

Inflammation doesn't fuse bones or dissolve cartilage in a few days, and the limit comes from swelling and pain, not every muscle tightening.

Takeaway: Signs of inflammation: redness, warmth, swelling, pain, loss of function.

questions.stem: Place the events of acute inflammation after an injury in order.
items: Damaged cells release chemicals like histamine and cytokines
Nearby vessels widen and become leaky
Chemokines call neutrophils, then macrophages, to the site
Germs and debris are cleared, and repair begins
questions.rationale:
Injury → chemical signals → wider, leaky vessels → redness, warmth, swelling → chemokines call neutrophils, then macrophages → clean-up and repair.

Putting the white cells before the vessel changes is a mistake: the vessels widen and loosen first, which lets the cells reach the tissue.

Takeaway: Signal, vessels open, signs appear, cells arrive, repair.

questions.stem: A client asks why a sprained ankle is inflamed when there's no infection. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “The swelling is from your immune system attacking the ankle's own tissue.”
“Sprains cause an allergy that looks like inflammation.”
“Some germs must have entered through the skin.”
“Inflammation is a response to any tissue injury, not just to germs.”
questions.rationale:
Inflammation answers any tissue injury, including a sprain, a burn, or a cut, whether or not germs are present.

An intact sprain has no entry for germs, it isn't an autoimmune attack, and it isn't an allergy.

Takeaway: Injury of any kind can set off inflammation.

questions.stem: A client's infected wound is getting worse. Which finding suggests the inflammation is now affecting the whole body?
options: Redness spreading slowly around the wound's edges
Mild swelling at the wound site
Warmth over the wound when touched
A fever with chills and a fast heart rate
questions.rationale:
Fever, chills, and a fast heart rate are systemic signs: the inflammatory chemicals are acting throughout the body, which needs prompt follow-up.

Redness, swelling, and warmth at the wound are local signs of inflammation.

Takeaway: Local: red, warm, swollen. Systemic: fever, chills, fast heart rate.

questions.stem: In the first hours after bacteria enter a cut, which white blood cells should the nurse expect to fill the site?
options: Lymphocytes
Eosinophils
Neutrophils
Basophils
questions.rationale:
Neutrophils are the most numerous white cells and the first to arrive at a bacterial infection, called by chemokines; macrophages follow.

Lymphocytes lead the slower, specific response, eosinophils rise with parasites and allergies, and basophils release histamine.

Takeaway: First hours: neutrophils. Later: macrophages and lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A client with a viral infection has a high lymphocyte count. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Lymphocytes are leaking out of the lymph nodes by mistake.”
“Lymphocytes rise to replace the red cells the virus destroyed.”
“Lymphocytes multiply to fight the virus and infected cells.”
“Lymphocytes rise because the virus is bacterial.”
questions.rationale:
Lymphocytes (T and B cells) lead the fight against viruses: T cells kill infected cells, and B cells make antibodies, so their count rises.

Viruses aren't bacteria, and a bacterial infection raises neutrophils more. Lymphocytes aren't leaking by mistake, and they don't replace red cells.

Takeaway: Bacteria: neutrophils up. Viruses: lymphocytes up.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the white blood cells. For each cell, click to specify its group.
rows: Neutrophil
Lymphocyte
Eosinophil
Monocyte
Basophil
questions.rationale:
Granulocytes, with granules in their cytoplasm, are the neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils. Agranulocytes are the lymphocytes and monocytes.

Calling monocytes granulocytes is a mistake: they're agranulocytes, which become macrophages in the tissues.

Takeaway: Granulocytes: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils. Agranulocytes: lymphocytes, monocytes.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's white blood cell differential. Which white cell should the nurse expect to be the most numerous?
options: Lymphocytes
Monocytes
Basophils
Neutrophils
questions.rationale:
Neutrophils make up about half to two-thirds of the white cells in the blood, the largest share.

Lymphocytes are second, and monocytes and basophils are a small share; basophils are the fewest.

Takeaway: Neutrophils are the most common white cell; basophils the least.

questions.stem: After an infection clears, which cells should the nurse expect to clean up the dead cells and debris?
options: Macrophages
Platelets
Plasma cells
Basophils
questions.rationale:
Macrophages (grown-up monocytes) engulf dead cells, worn-out neutrophils, and debris, clearing the way for repair.

Platelets plug vessels, plasma cells make antibodies, and basophils release histamine; none of them clears debris.

Takeaway: Macrophages: the clean-up crew.

questions.stem: A client's regulatory T cells aren't working properly. Which problem should the nurse expect to be more likely?
options: Frequent viral infections from too few cytotoxic T cells
The immune system attacking the body's own tissues
Severe bleeding from a lack of platelets
A lack of antibodies after vaccines
questions.rationale:
Regulatory T cells calm the immune response and keep it from attacking the body. Without them, autoimmune attacks on the body's own tissues become more likely.

Regulatory T cells don't make cytotoxic T cells, platelets, or antibodies.

Takeaway: Regulatory T cells: the immune system's brakes.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the white blood cells. Which of the following are lymphocytes?
options: Monocytes
Neutrophils
Mast cells
Innate lymphoid cells
B cells
T cells
questions.rationale:
Lymphocytes include T cells, B cells, and the innate lymphoid cells.

Neutrophils are granulocytes, monocytes are agranulocytes that become macrophages, and mast cells live in the tissues and release histamine.

Takeaway: Lymphocytes: T, B, and innate lymphoid cells.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing B cells. Which cells do B cells become when they make antibodies?
options: Plasma cells
Macrophages
Mast cells
Cytotoxic T cells
questions.rationale:
Activated B cells become plasma cells, which release large amounts of antibodies (and some become memory B cells).

Macrophages come from monocytes, mast cells are tissue cells that release histamine, and cytotoxic T cells develop from T cells.

Takeaway: B cell → plasma cell → antibodies.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing innate and adaptive immunity. Which example is an innate response, one that needs no earlier exposure?
options: Antibodies made after a measles vaccine
Memory B cells responding to a second exposure
Neutrophils engulfing bacteria at a new cut
Cytotoxic T cells trained against a specific virus
questions.rationale:
Innate defenses act right away against any germ, without earlier exposure: neutrophils engulfing bacteria at a new cut, inflammation, and barriers like the skin.

Antibodies, memory cells, and trained cytotoxic T cells belong to the adaptive response, which targets a specific germ and remembers it.

Takeaway: Innate: fast, general. Adaptive: slower, specific, with memory.

questions.stem: A client asks what a white blood cell differential shows. Which answer should the nurse give?
options: “The total number of red and white blood cells together.”
“The share of each type of white blood cell.”
“How quickly your white cells settle in a tube.”
“Whether your white cells carry enough oxygen.”
questions.rationale:
A differential breaks the white count into the share of each type: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils.

It doesn't count red cells. How fast cells settle is the sedimentation rate, and white cells don't carry oxygen.

Takeaway: Differential: which white cells, and how many of each.

questions.stem: A newborn has antibodies that came from the mother before birth. Which type of immunity is this?
options: Active immunity, which lasts for life
Passive immunity, which fades in a few months
Active immunity, made by the baby's own B cells
Passive immunity, which builds memory cells
questions.rationale:
Antibodies received from someone else give passive immunity: protection right away, but it fades over months, since the baby didn't make them or memory cells.

Active immunity comes from the person's own immune response, after infection or a vaccine. Passive immunity doesn't build memory cells.

Takeaway: Active: you make it, it lasts. Passive: you receive it, it fades.

questions.stem: A client asks why a booster dose of a vaccine is needed. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “It treats any infection you may have caught since your first dose was given.”
“It gives you the antibodies directly from someone else.”
“It replaces the first dose, which didn't work.”
“It reminds your memory cells and raises your antibody levels again.”
questions.rationale:
A booster re-exposes the immune system to the antigen, so memory cells respond quickly and antibody levels rise again for lasting protection.

The first dose did work; the booster builds on it. Vaccines prevent rather than treat, and receiving antibodies from someone else is passive immunity.

Takeaway: Boosters wake up memory cells.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing antibodies. How do antibodies stop a bacterial toxin from causing harm?
options: They bind the toxin so it can't attach to cells
They break the toxin down inside the liver's cells
They make the bacteria release less of the toxin
They carry the toxin out of the body in the urine
questions.rationale:
Antibodies bind to the toxin (neutralize it), so it can't attach to the body's cells; the antibody-toxin clump is then cleared.

Antibodies don't digest the toxin in the liver, control how much the bacteria make, or carry it into the urine.

Takeaway: Antibodies neutralize, mark, and clump germs and toxins.

questions.stem: A client doesn't know which vaccines they've had. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Give each vaccine again now, just to be safe
Skip the vaccines until the client remembers which ones
Help the client find and keep an immunization record
Order antibody tests for each vaccine-preventable disease
questions.rationale:
Keeping an immunization record (childhood, yearly flu and COVID-19, and pneumococcal and shingles for older adults) is part of immune health; the nurse helps the client find the record from past providers or the state registry.

Repeating every vaccine or testing for every disease isn't the first step, and skipping vaccines leaves the client unprotected.

Takeaway: Know the record before deciding which vaccines are due.

questions.stem: A client asks why the flu vaccine is given every year but the measles vaccine isn't. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Flu viruses change each year, so last year's antibodies may not match.”
“The measles vaccine is stronger than the flu vaccine.”
“Flu antibodies last about a week, and measles antibodies last for months.”
“Measles is no longer a risk, so its vaccine isn't needed.”
questions.rationale:
Flu viruses change from season to season, so the vaccine is updated yearly; the measles virus stays much the same, so childhood doses protect for life.

It isn't about strength. Flu protection lasts months rather than a week, and measles is still a risk, which is why the vaccine matters.

Takeaway: Changing virus: yearly vaccine.

questions.stem: The day after a vaccine, a client has a sore arm and a low fever. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “You've caught the disease from the vaccine.”
“Your immune system is responding and building protection.”
“You're allergic to the vaccine and shouldn't get the next dose.”
“The vaccine was given into a vein by mistake.”
questions.rationale:
A sore arm and a low fever are common signs that the immune system is responding: inflammation where the vaccine was given and cytokines that raise the temperature.

These mild reactions don't mean the disease was caught or that there's an allergy (which brings hives, swelling, or trouble breathing), and they don't point to a vein.

Takeaway: Mild soreness and fever: the immune system at work.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing immunity. For each example, click to specify the type of immunity it gives.
rows: Antibodies made after a measles infection
Antibodies a baby gets through breast milk
Antibodies made after a vaccine
Antibodies injected after an exposure, to protect right away
questions.rationale:
Active: the person's own B cells make the antibodies, after an infection or a vaccine. Passive: the antibodies come from someone else, through the placenta, breast milk, or an injection.

Calling a vaccine passive is a mistake: a vaccine makes the body build its own antibodies and memory.

Takeaway: Made yourself: active. Received: passive.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client had chickenpox as a child and now has shingles. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Shingles is an allergic reaction to the chickenpox vaccine you had.”
“Shingles comes from a different virus that older adults catch from each other.”
“You caught chickenpox again from a child who had it recently.”
“The chickenpox virus slept in your nerves and woke as your immunity weakened.”
questions.rationale:
After chickenpox, the virus stays dormant in the nerves. As immunity weakens with age, it can reactivate as shingles, which is why the shingles vaccine is recommended for older adults.

It isn't a new chickenpox infection or an allergy, and it's the same virus that causes chickenpox.

Takeaway: Shingles: the chickenpox virus waking up; vaccinate older adults.

questions.stem: A client has been under stress for months and is healing slowly from a minor wound. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Long-term high cortisol dampens the inflammation needed to heal.”
“Stress lowers your cortisol, which raises your blood sugar too high.”
“Cortisol speeds up the inflammation so much that it damages the wound.”
“Stress has no effect on healing; the wound must be infected.”
questions.rationale:
Cortisol, a steroid hormone, affects inflammation, metabolism, blood pressure, and sleep. Long-term stress keeps it high, which dampens the inflammatory and immune response a wound needs to heal.

Stress raises cortisol, which calms inflammation rather than speeding it up, and stress does affect healing.

Takeaway: High cortisol: less inflammation, slower healing, more infections.

questions.stem: A client's erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is high. Which interpretation should the nurse make?
options: It pinpoints an infection somewhere in the lungs
It shows that the infection is bacterial, not viral
Red cells are settling fast, a sign of inflammation
It means the client is dehydrated and needs fluids
questions.rationale:
The ESR measures how fast red cells settle in a tube; faster settling suggests inflammation somewhere in the body.

The ESR doesn't show where the inflammation is or whether an infection is bacterial (procalcitonin helps with that), and it isn't a test of hydration.

Takeaway: High ESR: inflammation is present, location unknown.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing interleukin-8 (IL-8). Which cells does IL-8 mainly call to an infection?
options: Neutrophils
Red blood cells
Platelets
Plasma cells
questions.rationale:
IL-8 is a chemokine that calls neutrophils to the site of infection or injury.

Red cells and platelets aren't called by chemokines to fight infection, and plasma cells stay in the lymphoid tissue making antibodies.

Takeaway: IL-8: a neutrophil magnet.

questions.stem: A client's C-reactive protein (CRP) is high. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The client has a bacterial infection somewhere in the lungs
Inflammation is present, and more tests are needed to find where
The client has prostate cancer that needs a biopsy
The client's inflammation has ended, so no follow-up is needed now
questions.rationale:
CRP rises with inflammation anywhere in the body. It shows that inflammation is present, but not where or why, so other findings and tests are needed.

A high CRP doesn't point to the lungs or to a bacterial cause by itself, it isn't a cancer test, and it rises with active inflammation, not after it ends.

Takeaway: Inflammatory markers: yes or no, not where.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old client's PSA is mildly high. His prostate is enlarged but smooth, and a biopsy found no cancer. Which condition most likely explains the PSA?
options: A kidney infection
Prostatitis from a bacterial infection
Benign prostatic hyperplasia
Prostate cancer that the biopsy missed
questions.rationale:
PSA is made by normal and cancerous prostate cells. A smooth, enlarged prostate with a negative biopsy fits benign prostatic hyperplasia, a common benign cause.

Prostatitis brings a tender prostate, fever, and painful urination. Cancer isn't ruled out forever, but it isn't the most likely cause here. A kidney infection doesn't raise PSA.

Takeaway: High PSA: cancer, BPH, or prostatitis; it needs follow-up, not alarm.

questions.stem: A client asks which cells make prostate-specific antigen (PSA). Which answer should the nurse give?
options: “Cells of the bladder lining.”
“Cancer cells in the prostate, and no others.”
“Normal and cancerous prostate cells.”
“White blood cells fighting a prostate infection.”
questions.rationale:
PSA is a protein made by normal and cancerous prostate cells, which is why benign conditions can raise it too.

Cancer cells alone is a common misunderstanding: normal prostate cells make PSA too. It isn't made by white cells or the bladder.

Takeaway: PSA comes from the prostate itself, healthy or not.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the sedimentation rate. Why do red cells settle faster when there's inflammation?
options: Inflammation makes the red cells much smaller
Proteins like fibrinogen make the red cells clump, so they sink faster
Inflammation destroys the red cells, so they break into heavy pieces
The fever thins the plasma, so the cells fall through it faster
questions.rationale:
During inflammation, fibrinogen and other proteins rise and make red cells stick together; the clumps sink faster in the tube.

The red cells don't shrink, break apart, or fall through a thinned plasma.

Takeaway: More inflammatory proteins → red cells clump → faster settling.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching about exercise for immune health. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The goal is about {{0}} minutes of exercise a week, such as {{1}} minutes on 5 to 7 days.

options: 5 to 10

questions.rationale:
The instructor's goal: about 150 minutes a week, or 20 to 30 minutes on 5 to 7 days.

Choosing 60 to 90 minutes a day is a mistake: it's far more than the goal, which most clients can reach with 20 to 30 minutes on most days.

Takeaway: Immune health: 150 minutes a week.

questions.stem: A client asks which way of eating best supports the immune system. Which answer should the nurse give?
options: “Mostly packaged snacks with vitamins added to them.”
“Whole foods, like vegetables, fruits, and whole grains.”
“Energy drinks for the extra B vitamins they contain.”
“A high-sugar diet that gives you quick energy for the day.”
questions.rationale:
A diet of whole foods supports immune health, one of the instructor's interventions.

Packaged snacks, energy drinks, and high-sugar foods add sugar and artificial ingredients that can drive inflammation.

Takeaway: Whole foods help; sugar and energy drinks hurt.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing four clients' vaccine records. Which client should the nurse remind about the shingles vaccine?
options: A 9-year-old who is due for school vaccines
A 32-year-old who is pregnant
A 25-year-old who had chickenpox at age 6
A 67-year-old who had chickenpox as a child
questions.rationale:
The shingles vaccine is recommended for older adults, in whom the dormant chickenpox virus is more likely to reactivate.

Younger adults, children, and pregnant clients aren't the group the shingles vaccine is meant for.

Takeaway: Older adults: shingles and pneumococcal vaccines, plus yearly flu and COVID-19.

questions.stem: A healthy adult asks which vaccines are needed every year. Which answer should the nurse give?
options: “Tetanus and shingles.”
“Pneumococcal and hepatitis B.”
“Flu and COVID-19.”
“Measles and mumps.”
questions.rationale:
The instructor's list of yearly vaccines: flu and COVID-19.

Measles and mumps are childhood vaccines, and the shingles and pneumococcal vaccines are for older adults; none of them is yearly.

Takeaway: Every year: flu and COVID-19.

questions.stem: A client wants to start an herbal supplement for the immune system and also takes several prescribed medicines. Which response should the nurse give?
options: “Herbal supplements are natural, so they're safe to start right away.”
“Ask your provider first, since supplements can interact with medicines.”
“Stop taking your prescribed medicines for a while as you try the supplement.”
“Take twice the label dose to get a stronger effect on your immunity.”
questions.rationale:
Herbal supplements can be part of healthy choices with provider guidance: some interact with prescribed medicines, so the provider should know first.

Natural doesn't mean safe, stopping prescribed medicines could be dangerous, and doubling the dose adds risk.

Takeaway: Supplements: with the provider's guidance, never in place of care.

questions.stem: A client with diabetes asks why the flu vaccine matters more for them. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “Diabetes weakens your immune response, so flu can be serious.”
“The flu vaccine lowers your blood glucose level for the winter.”
“People with diabetes can catch the flu from the vaccine itself.”
“The vaccine replaces your other diabetes care.”
questions.rationale:
Chronic conditions like diabetes weaken the immune response, so the flu and its complications can be more serious; the yearly vaccine lowers that risk.

The vaccine doesn't lower glucose or replace diabetes care, and it can't cause the flu.

Takeaway: Chronic illness: more reason for yearly vaccines.

questions.stem: A client asks why older adults are offered extra vaccines. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “The immune system weakens with age, so infections hit harder.”
“Older adults' childhood vaccines wear off and stop working.”
“Extra vaccines replace the need for exercise and a healthy diet.”
“Pneumonia is a risk that starts after age 65.”
questions.rationale:
The immune system weakens with age, so infections like pneumonia and shingles are more common and more dangerous; that's why older adults are offered the pneumococcal and shingles vaccines.

Childhood vaccines don't all stop working, vaccines don't replace exercise and diet, and pneumonia can strike at any age.

Takeaway: Aging immune system: more vaccines, plus healthy habits.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a client's habits. For each habit, click to specify its effect on immune health.
rows: Walking 30 minutes, 5 days a week
Drinking three energy drinks a day
Eating vegetables and whole grains
Skipping the yearly flu vaccine
Starting an herbal supplement without telling the provider
Keeping an immunization record
questions.rationale:
Regular exercise, whole foods, and an up-to-date immunization record support immune health. Energy drinks add sugar and artificial ingredients that drive inflammation, skipping the flu vaccine leaves the client unprotected, and a supplement without the provider's guidance can interact with medicines.

Calling any supplement helpful is a mistake: supplements belong with provider guidance, as part of other healthy choices.

Takeaway: Move, eat whole foods, vaccinate, and talk to the provider.
